utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are no preliminary matters to be raised immediately, if I understand well. Therefore, the witness may be escorted into the courtroom. Yes, there is, however, one matter which is about scheduling in January. We discussed it earlier. The Chamber announces that for reasons related to the scheduling of witnesses, the week of the 12th of January shall be a non-sitting week and that in the week following, that we'll sit for the full five days of that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Runjevac. Perhaps needless to do but I still want to remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still want to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Stojanovic, I think you had put all your questions to the witness but you were still -- you still have to read a short summary - a short summary, I say - of the testimony of this witness as found in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I tried to make it short as agreed, and I hope that I will keep to the number of lines that you gave us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rato Runjevac is a lawyer who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the interpreters have not received a text, so therefore would you please read at decent speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honours. Although I think that I gave the summary yesterday. It's the same text. Very well. He's a lawyer who happened to be in Sarajevo when the war broke out. At the time, he was the senior public prosecutor. On the 21st of May, 1992, he notes that with the arrival of the national parties and when they took up power at the republican level, people started taking over positions in the justice system but his position remained the same. At the time in the city of Sarajevo, the greatest problems were posed by armed incidents and drug trades, and these acts were committed by Juka Prazina, Celo Bajramovic, and others, due to which as part of his duties he sought that meetings be held of all relevant prosecutors and the B and H MUP in order to step up activities relating to the issuance of criminal reports and the criminal prosecution of persons who were making the security situation worse. He's going to talk about specific examples of the different views of the reasons for the disruption of the security situation in Rogatica and Sokolac and the opportunistic attitude of the local authorities regarding incidents caused by Juka Prazina in Sarajevo, as well as the fact that nothing was done and there were no criminal proceedings against the brothers Sabanovic in Visegrad. He will also talk about the support that these persons received from Alija Izetbegovic instead of him actually insisting that they should be criminally charged. He notes that following the well-known incident when the Serbian best man was killed in Bascarsija, he asked the authorised public prosecutor's office in Sarajevo to provide him the case files regarding this incident. And then in the police part of the case, he could see that witnesses recognised the person who fired the shots but the policemen released that person. In the meantime, the rump B and H Parliament decided anti-constitutionally to hold a referendum on independence, and this caused inter-ethnic tensions to rise to the ultimate degree. So in view of the experiences with the barricades, people started taking their families out of Sarajevo and then they would return to Sarajevo. The witness himself decided to do that. Also, in those days in April 1992, he noticed armed people in Sarajevo. He could see that there was shooting all over town. He received information that there were first casualties. He was threatened by his neighbour that he would be killed for no reason at all. And on the eve of the 1st of May holiday, he decided to go to the village where his children were, his children invited him to do that. On the way there he saw a number of check-points near villages with armed people, both Serb and Bosniak ones. Since he could no longer return to his job because of the escalating conflict, he remained in Trebinje until the end of the war. Your Honours, this was the summary of the statement for Witness Rato Runjevac, and I would like to thank the witness for answering my questions. This would be the end of our presentation regarding this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Witness, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. File. You find him to your right, and Mr. File is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Runjevac.

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to begin by asking you a few questions about your background. You discuss your professional background in paragraph 2 of your statement. There the only mention of any time that you spent in the military is where you say you completed your military service in June 1975. So is it correct to say that the only time you were in the military was in 1975 or earlier?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not in the army before 1975. I was in the army in 1974, in Osinjak, that's where I served my military term of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you were never employed in the military justice system; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before or after? [In English] No. [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would like to turn your attention to paragraph 19 of your statement; specifically, the part where you refer to seeing two of your neighbours with guns that they should not have had, as you say. And then you conclude the paragraph stating: "All this told me that my Bosniak neighbours had long had their sources for purchasing weapons that civilians could not have according to the law, only authorised officials."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is D860 in e-court. For reference it's page 9 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, my question for you is: Here are you drawing a conclusion about all of your Bosnian Muslim neighbours or just the two that you saw with weapons?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw the two of them with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you did not know how these individuals obtained these weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add this: This other person that had this American pump-action rifle was my neighbour. We often spent time together, visited each other. And before the war, he showed me a wood-burning stove in his apartment, which in the Bosnian is called "bubnjara," which was indicative to me, why would you need a wood-burning stove in an apartment that had central heating? So that was a little bit strange to me. It didn't seem to make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, for the moment I'm just asking you about the -- the weapons that you saw. You also did not know how long these two individuals had had those weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of your whereabouts, you left Sarajevo on or before the 30th of April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I took my children on the 3rd of April, this was before the international recognition, because there was panic about what would happen in the town once there was international recognition. This was particularly prominent among my colleagues, mothers, so that I decided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there for a moment. Could you please focus your answers on what is asked because part of your answer you're giving now is, first of all, not a direct answer to the question; and secondly, it is already in your statement. So therefore, it's repetitious. Please proceed, Mr. File. And I think the question was that you left -- and the question is about you, that you left on or before the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you did not return after that; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you also did not execute any of your functions as senior public prosecutor in Sarajevo after the 30th of April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you were removed from that position on the 21st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And the reason given for that was wilful abandonment of your duty and work obligations; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the reasons given.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter number 31808, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So I'm just going to direct your attention to the lower left-hand portion of the page in B/C/S. You'll see that this is from the Official Gazette of RBiH. It's a decision to relieve of duty the senior public prosecutor in Sarajevo, and it says: "Rato Runjevac is hereby relieved of duty of the Sarajevo Senior Public Prosecutor due to wilful abandonment of his duty and work obligations at the Senior Public Prosecutor's Office in Sarajevo." Now, is this consistent with your understanding of why you were removed from duty?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did receive this decision -- I never received it. Secondly, it is not true that I wilfully abandoned my work because I'd returned in early April, once I left my children in Trebinje, which was my intention, to return after the 1st of May holidays, which lasted for four or five days. Perhaps you know that on the 2nd of May - and I remember this very well because it was my birthday on the 3rd of May - when I meant to return -- I meant to return on Sunday, which was the last day of the holiday, there was a general attack and defence actions in Sarajevo. Due to the war there was a lot of destruction, and it was when I decided that I could not return to Sarajevo without putting my life and security in danger. When I tried to leave, they had already tried to mobilise me at the check-point in Lukavica and it was difficult to leave, never mind to come back after a few days -- or rather, after a month. Since the post office building in Sarajevo was burning, all the telephone lines were cut on the 2nd of May, but I managed to use special lines of the electricity utility company from Trebinje, and I managed to reach my secretary, Zdravka, and to tell her that I could not return for objective reasons. Of course, I was not only one in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many parents were in that situation. Excuse me. All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document and I would have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 13808 receives Exhibit Number P7014, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. I would have one or not more than a few questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to paragraph 15 of your statement. Could it be shown on the screen. And that is P -- D860. I think it would be page 6 in -- the end of paragraph 15 in both languages. Yes. You describe in that paragraph the act and conduct of a certain Mr. Sabanovic, and then at the very end you -- the last sentence reads: "The public knows about this because it was broadcast on television together with the fact that Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the BH Presidency, appealed to him and supported him, instead of insisting on him being prosecuted." Now, you say the public knows about this. Do you consider yourself to be a member of the public and therefore you learned about it through the media? Is that -- or do you say: The public knew it because they watched television and I knew it for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, that incident was broadcast live by Television Sarajevo or the Bosnia-Herzegovina television, so the dialogue between that gentleman and the president of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, everybody could follow it on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First could you tell us when it happened? Because that's totally unclear from the -- from the statement. When exactly did it happen?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot say exactly if it was March or April. Perhaps it was in May when I was watching television in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was after you had left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you watch it on television and that's the source of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now just for me to understand, apparently there was a violent exchange. And then you say it was live broadcasted. Should I understand negotiations between Mr. Sabanovic and the government? And where was Mr. Izetbegovic at the time? I mean, I'm just trying to get an impression on what exactly happened. Was it by telephone that they communicated?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, what probably happened was the TV station at the time was called Yutel and it frequently tried to calm the situation down. Mr. Milic, everybody who worked at that television station. So I think that there was a contact, phone contact between him and the person who was at the hydroelectric power-plant. And they also linked up Mr. Izetbegovic from the presidency so that he could try to get Mr. Sabanovic not to do what he was threatening to do, which was to destroy the dam. The link was a telephone link and that conversation was broadcast live on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier you said: "So I think that there was a contact, phone contact ..." Do you think that that was the case or do you -- why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so because they managed to establish a connection with Mr. Sabanovic at the hydroelectric power-plant by telephone, and then they were looking for a way to influence him so that he would not carry out his threat. And then they asked Mr. Alija Izetbegovic to speak with him on the telephone, and all of that was broadcast live on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what exactly did Mr. Izetbegovic tell Mr. Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that after 22 years or more. All I know is that he had a positive effect on him so that he did not do that. He was explaining why he wanted to do that. So he was telling Mr. Sabanovic that he understood him, his reasons and everything, but he was trying to get him not to do what he was intending to do because of the danger that was posed by that down river for the people there. So Alija Izetbegovic had a positive effect and he used his position and his authority to get Mr. Sabanovic not to do what he was intending to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you also say in your statement that he "appealed to him and supported him, instead of insisting on him being prosecuted." Would you expect Mr. Izetbegovic at that moment to say to

utterances.speaker: MR. SABANOVIC
utterances.text: You'll be prosecuted if you go on? Is that what you -- rather than to calm him down in whatever way. I'm puzzled by the statement in this respect.

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in our situation in terms of crime and security, the idea was to calm the situation down, to give him support, and not to threaten him. However, when the crime was committed, when owing to his activity - I mean, Mr. Izetbegovic - he didn't do that, and I believe that after that, at his request as a member and the president of the highest Executive Board, which was the presidency, they should have given an order for the crime to be prosecuted. However, I don't believe that that ever transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think you don't believe that. Any reason for that belief?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe because immediately after the events, and also for objective reasons - i.e., the war - I did not hear or I did not read anywhere that any of those crimes were ever prosecuted; for example, the destruction of the sculpture of Ivo Andric, the events at the dam, the barricades, the murder of the wedding party member, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the sentence I read to you suggests that Izetbegovic could be heard on television not insisting on Mr. Sabanovic being prosecuted, but I do understand that that part of the sentence, the very last part, relates to that you believe that he was not prosecuted because you never heard he was prosecuted, and what the role of Mr. Izetbegovic was at that time is -- you couldn't know that from watching television, at least not the live broadcast of the event. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question. Sir, at the time who -- which authority was responsible for initiating prosecutions against criminals?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both then and now it would be the police, the Ministry of the Interior, and those who actually initiate prosecution are state prosecutions. The point of my statement was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking --

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for a year and a half I never received anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the point of your statement. I am just asking you a simple question. You have answered my question. So it would not be Izetbegovic's duty to initiate prosecutions, isn't it so? It was for you, the prosecutor, to do so.

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then -- one last question. You had left Sarajevo already at that point in time and were not actually functioning as a prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so but let me just say that the municipal or, rather, basic prosecutor in Visegrad was responsible for this, for the prosecution of this crime. He should have done it on a report received by the police. I don't know whether he ever received it or not. And it was up to the prosecutor to prosecute, and I did it all that time without any criminal reports as a matter of fact. I did it as means of preemption to prevent any escalations of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you have no specific knowledge on how it happened that he was not prosecuted, what exactly -- how the decision-making process took place because you were not there.

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing specific. But those organs were obstructed in the work along party lines because the parties took over not only in the ministries but also in the executive power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that as a general matter. But no specific knowledge about this decision, if there was any, which resulted in the non-prosecution of Mr. Sabanovic. I have no further questions. Any questions triggered by -- Mr. Stojanovic, no further questions. Mr. File --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- no further questions. Then, Mr. Runjevac, this concludes your testimony in this court. It may have been relatively short, but as I reminded you several times, we have your statement and of course that's the main body of the evidence you have given. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague, for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for having listened to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next witness to be called, no protective measures, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's Mr. Boro Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Boro Tadic. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: May I be excused, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused, Mr. File. Mr. Tieger, is it -- we're just discussing, was it Mr. File's first appearances today in court? Yesterday, of course. I mean yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. He'd been introduced to the Chamber during the testimony of Witness Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we have to be ashamed of ourselves to have forgotten about that. But at least the matter is clear and I do understand that the Prosecution is following good standards to introduce new counsel. Good morning, Mr. Tadic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Godspeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Boro Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, have you provided a statement to the Radovan Karadzic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And based on that statement, have you also spoken to the General Mladic Defence team and have you provided a statement to them as well?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D1616.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you have that document on the screen before you. Do you recognise the signature on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see a signature again?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise it? Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we reviewed this statement, would you say that everything has been recorded correctly?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to your best knowledge, what is contained in this statement, is everything true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, true and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01616 receives Exhibit Number D861, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if the same questions would be put to you today, would you in substance give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D861 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, it happened several times over the last few weeks that the logical sequence, first question is: Does the document reflect what you said; second, did you give that information to the best of your knowledge; third question, would you give the same answers if being asked the same questions today. That's the sequence which is -- we're losing parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm always grateful for your help, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. The matter has been repaired. Please move on with -- if you have any questions or perhaps you would prefer to start reading the summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will first read statement summary, Your Honours, and I will have only a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the war broke out in Croatia, the 6th Partizan Brigade was mobilised in Sanski Most municipality. The brigade commander was Colonel Branko Basara, and Mr. Boro Tadic was the commander of the 1st Battalion. In the spring of 1992, the general security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina deteriorated, inter-ethnic tensions escalated, the conflict from the territory of Croatia split into B and H and the situation worsened by the day. For this reason a decision was made and in the early April of 1992, the 6th Krajina Brigade of the JNA was brought back from Western Slavonia to the area of Sanski Most. Members of the unit mobilised in the area of Sanski Most were not professional military personnel; rather, they were local people. Before the start of the war in Bosnia, Mr. Tadic has personally taken part in discussions with the Muslims, and he went to the Muslim villages explaining that peace should be preserved. Before the war, Muslims and Croats were arming illegally and organising a paramilitary force. Even though some of them responded to mobilisation in 1991, they were increasingly leaving the unit. They also ignored the call to surrender illegal weapons and instead attacked the soldiers and police who were tasked with disarming them. At no point was the policy of the SDS or the VRS to remove permanently the Muslims and Croats from B and H territory to which the Bosnian Serbs claimed right. The Serbs sought for a long time a formula for coexistence and for the survival of the common country and its preservation. Mr. Tadic knows that municipal authorities distributed humanitarian aid equally to all those who were in need, regardless of their ethnic or religious background. That was statement summary, and I would have only couple of questions for Mr. Tadic. With your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, were you a member of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina at one point?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1986 to 1990. That was the last Communist assembly, the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the eve of multiparty elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in the founding of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind my speeches at the sessions of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after I had realised that there was a project and an intention for my state to disintegrate, to be broken up, and when I had realised that I was isolated and that those who were with me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I am stopping you there. You are apparently giving reasons for whatever will follow. The question was: Did you participate in the founding of the SDS? Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm trying to say is that it was only natural --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for me to say what I was saying at the assembly sessions at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that is not the question. Whether it's natural what you said or not is not what you are asked to tell us. You were asked to tell us whether you participated in the founding of the SDS. Did you participate in the founding or did you not participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did participate in the founding of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an answer to the question. Listen carefully to the next question Mr. Lukic will put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us the reasons why you participated in the founding of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I realised already as a member of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in 1988, 1989, and 1990, that the years ahead of us would be very grave. When I realised that the Muslims had set up their own party and that the Croats had established their own party, I participated in the founding of the Serbian Democratic Party during the first month or so. But my condition was not to be a party member, bearing in mind that my wish was to be free from any political chains, because my faith in God forbade me to be a slave to another man as I was a slave to Tito in the Communist Party during the communist rule. I didn't want that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDS or not?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you what your positions were in 1992, from the beginning of 1992 until the end?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: In early 1992 I was the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 6th Sana Brigade in Jasenovac. I became sick in January and February, and I ended up in the military hospital in Sarajevo on the 17th of March, and I stayed there until the 2nd of April. What happened was that my return from Sarajevo through the barricades that had already been set up, and I saw with my own eyes that Muslim and Croat flags were tied, the night that I returned, the brigade from Jasenovac returned as well, and then the brigade commander appointed me as his assistant for morale and religious affairs. I performed those duties in the course of April and May 1992. In May 1992, I heard from the commander that those people from the municipality suggested that I should be the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence. However, at that time I was not in Sanski Most often because I couldn't pass through Muslim villages. It was only at the end of May that I realised what was being proposed. Up to the month of July, I was the secretary for the Secretariat of National Defence, and as of August I was the chief of the Department of National Defence for Sanski Most, and I stayed in that position until the 1st of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please speak slowly, sir. The interpreters are desperately trying to keep pace with you and they are finding it very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what I mean when I make this gesture, as I did several times, and you saw it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And one more thing: When you were appointed assistant commander for morale and religious affairs, did you continue serving as the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: While I was in hospital while I was sick, another person was appointed and replaced me. And as soon as I returned, the battalion commander who was appointed remained at that position, and I was given another role as assistant commander for morale and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Tadic. This is all we had for you at this moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just don't understand the very last answer, Mr. Lukic. Sir, you say when you came back from hospital, the person who had been appointed to replace you continued in the post of assistant commander for religious affairs and -- morale and religious affairs. And then you say also that you were given another post, but then you call it by the same name. What post were you placed in now when you came from hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the commander of the 1st Battalion before I was hospitalised. And then while I was hospitalised another person was appointed as the battalion commander. When I returned from hospital, which coincided with the return of the brigade from Jasenovac to Sanski Most, I was appointed as assistant commander for morale and religious affairs. The person who had been appointed in my place continued serving as the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I can just follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Mr. Tadic can just give us the name, if he knows, if he remembers.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Brane Cicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again can you repeat the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Brane Cicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. Once again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. You will find Mr. Jeremy to your right, and Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. And may I urge you to focus your answer on what is asked, rather than to move in all directions. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I would like to begin, just in the couple of minutes that we have, by returning to something that you said this morning. So if I understand correctly, you were a founding member of the Serbian Democratic Party, or the SDS, but you were not in fact a member of that party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: The conversation with those who initiated the foundation of the party started by me saying, "I will help in the setting up of the Serbian Democratic Party as a movement of the Serbian people to preserve Yugoslavia on one condition: I don't want to be a party member." Mr. Sendic, who was my collocutor, accepted that. I did participate in the founding of the party but with the reservation, with the caveat that I would never hold a position, I would never work as a party member, but I said that I will invest all of my potentials in preserving Yugoslavia and in the project which was the political platform of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. And the last question on this area is this: Now, together with Radovan Karadzic you arranged for a gathering of the SDS in September 1990 in Lusci Palanka that was attended by him and various other leaders of the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: During the month when the party was being established I was in constant contact and I happened to be together with Radovan twice. For the first time it was in 1990 and the second time was on the 9th of September, 1992, in Lusci Palanka --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when he and Raskovic were there. In other words, I took part in the organising of that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know we are at break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break first. Mr. Tadic, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after the break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. There was one preliminary matter which we should deal with before the next witness arrives, but I don't know how much time it would take. If it is a matter of -- that's at least our information, that before Mr. Milutinovic would arrive that we would have to deal with a preliminary matter. But if it takes more than half a minute or minute, then I would postpone it. If it is dealt with in a second, then we'd hear it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It will take longer than a half a minute, not much but sufficiently more that we should proceed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we proceed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Tieger was speaking and not Mr. Traldi. Now it's corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you testified in the Karadzic case in December 2013; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you told the truth in that testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, your statement in the Karadzic case took the form of question and answer. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to do now is to look at one of the questions and one of the answers that you provided in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we therefore please see 65 ter 1D02286. And that's Mr. Tadic's statement from the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tadic. So we see that this is your statement. We see your name on the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 3, and I'd like to look at question 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'll note that paragraph 12 and 13 of the Karadzic statement are very similar in substance to paragraphs 11 and 12 of your Mladic statement. But I'd like to focus now on paragraph 14, and I'll read the question and the answer, and I'll ask you if you stand by that answer in respect of your testimony in this case. So the question is as follows: "Did the shortage of the professional command personnel influence the quality of command and control in the unit mobilised in the Sanski Most area?"

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the answer: "No, not to a significant degree. Reserve officers were generally trained for certain levels of command. They took courses and were called for tactical exercises that the JNA organised, and this training was of high standard." So simply, Mr. Tadic, do you stand by the answer that you provided to that question today?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I'm finished with the Karadzic statement, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, in paragraph 21 of your statement you discuss propaganda, and I'd like to ask you few questions on that topic now. Now, in 1992, the SDS produced a bulletin called the "Informator"; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I'd like to take a look at that with you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 06616 on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I think we're still waiting for it to come up, so 06616, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That still seems not to be the document. Could everyone verify whether he's using the right numbers, either by asking or in responding to the request?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And could you repeat the number of the document you are looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking for document number 06616, according to my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The 65 ter number of the statement of the witness is quite similar, but this bears 1D1616, but this is not what we are looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have the right document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- now on our screen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Thank you for your patience, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, on our screen before us we see the "Informator" of Serbian Democratic Party Sanski Most. And we see it's published on St. Peter's Day 1992. Now, St. Peter's Day is in July; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we see that the publisher of this document is the Serbian Democratic Party Information and Promotion Centre. Now, below that we see editor-in-chief Borislav Savanovic. Now, he was the president of the club of the SDS deputies in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And looking at the associates below that, we see R. Nedjeljko, that's a reference to Nedjeljko Rasula; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And he was president of the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now we also see a reference to Boro Tadic as one of the associates. That's you, right?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And so you contributed to this publication; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we see at the bottom of the page that it was printed in 300 copies. Now, the target audience of the "Informator" was not just SDS members but also Serbs and non-Serbs in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It was up to the people to read if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But it was generally available; yes?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whoever could get their hands on it could read it and inform themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like now to move to the content of this document. But before I do, I'd just want to remind you what you said in paragraph 21 of your statement, which is as follows: "It is bizarre to talk about the Serbian propaganda at the time as allegedly disseminating hatred and fear." And then at the end of that paragraph 21, you go on to say that the Serbs tried to "calm down the situation and prevent conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, could we go to page 3 in this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, we see that this section begins: "Dear brother Serbs ..." And I'll read a part of it. "Do you know what our blood-thirsty enemies have been scheming for us? "What they had in mind was to gouge out our eyes and carve us up, hack our bodies to pieces, rape women and girls in front of their dearest, to circumcise, to destroy our religion, to crush us - just because we happen to be Serbs. "Don't think that anybody's family would have been spared. They had monsters ready and committed to raping Serbian women, and they had developed a system of killing each and every Serb." And I'll skip down a few paragraphs to the eighth paragraph down, where we read: "They had been preparing for genocide against the Serbs, but did not get away with it because we saw what was coming. We warned and prepared our people in time." Now, Mr. Tadic, this is propaganda intended to disseminate hatred and fear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: When one discusses the truth, it is no propaganda aimed at misleading but rather to illuminate so that people would understand what is possible to happen. Everything what Rasula wrote had to do with some documents he showed me in the office. They found it in the possession of the SDS [as interpreted]. He even mentioned some instruments they found during their searches and their plans in terms of who was supposed to do what. Given the fact that we had gone through it all 50 years before in 1941, when only in one day five and a half thousand Serbs were killed and when thousands upon thousands of people from Sana were taken to Jasenovac, those wounds - which had still not healed - served as a warning for us, that we need to organise ourselves, and that we do not allow what happened in 1941 to happen again. As for the breakup of Yugoslavia, well, the Western world employed its cunning manner in that and we tried to pre-empt it. We were no longer the same people --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: -- who saw the genocide and slaughter of 1941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I just -- I do understand that you say it's not propaganda because it's the truth. That is, in brief, your answer to the question. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe witness should answer your questions first. I just have one intervention into -- into transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But is that well understood, your answer which I would just summarise in this way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would have another question, but first, Mr. Lukic, I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 31 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- line 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that wrong party was recorded. Maybe it should be clarified. "In possession of ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, yes. The documents that Mr. Rasula showed you in his office, they found it in the possession of, may I take it that you want to refer to in possession of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In his office, I don't recall the day exactly, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no -- just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- since I was away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the problem was that it was recorded as "SDS" but you referred to, which seems to be logical, the SDA. I have one short question. I thought you had confirmed that already but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I hope I said the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then one simple question. You also said in paragraph 21: "They tried to calm down the situation." The language you just saw on your screen, do you consider that language which would be useful to calm down the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was much propaganda coming from the West against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that's not my question. My question is: Whether the language that was just shown to you, whether you consider that language of a type to calm down the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a response to what was forthcoming, the breakup of Yugoslavia. No one was having it easy at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, for one reason or another you prefer rather not to answer my question. Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now -- so I'd like to look at another part of this document, and it's a part that is explicitly authored by Mr. Rasula --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, may I interrupt you. I'm terribly sorry to do this. I would like -- I have got a question related to just what the witness has just been saying. Sir, as an associate member of the "Informator," which is an organ of the SDS, you were working for the SDS, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I attended only one meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I stop you there. As a contributor to the "Informator" by virtue of being of an associate member, you were working for the SDS, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain the way the establishment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I don't want you to explain -- no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- went and developed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking you a very simple question. You can answer me "yes" or "no." Were you working for the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked for the Serbian people. If that included the SDS, then, yes, I helped wherever I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I helped in the establishment of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am not talking about the establishment. I am talking about contributing to the "Informator." That was an SDS organ. So by being -- you were contributing to the work of the SDS, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm asking you this question because at page 24, lines 8 to 17 are too long to mention but I'm just going to mention one line. At line 12 you say: "I did participate in the founding of the party but with the reservation, with the caveat that I would never hold a position, I would never work as a party member."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is not correct because now here you're working as an associate member of an organ of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as an associate but not as a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we please go to page 5 in the English of this document and page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tadic, this is a section written by Mr. Rasula and we see the title is: "The Place and the Role of the Serbian Democratic Party in Time of War."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And actually we'll need to -- having established the title, I'll need to go to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like you to focus on the seventh paragraph down on -- of the B/C/S on the screen before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And it's the third paragraph on the screen in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "With the coming of war and the new conditions, but still adhering to the goal of creating a Serbian state, the work of the Serbian Democratic Party naturally evolved into a series of duties and actions which served to prepare, organise, and provide the Serbian people with the means of guaranteeing their safety in Bosnia and Herzegovina, making them ready for a bitter battle with the other two peoples - the Muslims, if they are -- if indeed they are a people (THEY ARE NOT), and the Croats who have forever carried in their genes a sick, a pathological desire and urge to kill those better, more honest, and - do we need to say this - stronger than they are. It has always been like that." Mr. Tadic, you shared Mr. Rasula's views on Muslims and Croats; yes?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: His wording was much harder, much fiercer. My position is the position of faith. It is a fact that in all world wars, the Muslims and Croats turned on the Serbs and they always leaned towards Austria-Hungary, Turkey, and Germany, and this time around America. America took upon itself the role previously held by Germany in World War II on the eve of World War III.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I think we have a part of this in your statement and I'll come to it and you'll have an opportunity to address it. Now, from the answer that you just provided, I understand that you considered the words of Mr. Rasula to be stronger than the words that you would use. But substantively in terms of the gist of what we read here, do you agree or do you disagree with Mr. Rasula's position?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I do not agree with his wording and the way he used those words, but I do agree that there was a danger, a threat to us should they have been able to use force. Thank God they were not able to use force because they left the JNA which in turn resulted in the creation of a Serb army. It was their policy to abandon the JNA and leave Yugoslavia. This enabled the Serbs who remained legally in their state defending the constitutional order of Yugoslavia to get hold of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: That was the only possibility given to the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So when Mr. Rasula says that the Muslims are not a people, do you agree -- do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: You see, all documents that we have from the time of war and since refer to Bosniaks, but they are nowhere to be found. They called themselves Muslims before 1991. This shows you that they are confused in their understanding of themselves. Mesa Selimovic who was a Muslim but realised that he had Serb origins said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to stop you there again. You were asked whether you considered the Muslims to be a people or not. You are explaining us how they considered themselves, but the question was whether you considered them to be a people, yes or no. Would you please focus on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I respect whatever they say about themselves. If they say they are Bosniaks, I honour that. And I honoured when they called themselves Muslims. But what I think about that is a different matter. I respect someone who respects themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked about whether you have an opinion about that and what that opinion is. And by saying that "I respect whatever they say and my opinion I'll keep it for myself" is not an answer to the question. But that seems to be a pattern, that you're not answering the questions, and I would urge you to answer them. Now, in view of the last few questions put to you by Mr. Jeremy, whether you agreed with the views of Mr. Rasula, you used a lot words. But it's clear, or at least as I read it, and if -- as one could read it, in this text Mr. Rasula, by referring to genes, by referring to pathology, and by referring to the Serbs being better, depicts the Muslims as inferior people. Now, whatever political stance they may have taken in the past, do you agree - apart from the specific language - that -- with Mr. Rasula, that Muslims are inferior to Serbs? Because that's what appears from this text. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I said it was too hard-line. I would never put it in that way. But it's clear to me where the fear and the hate comes from and how come that they were always against the Serbs. Because these are Serbs who changed their faith and I was -- and they felt sorry once Turkey left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you do not share the view as expressed by Mr. Rasula in this text that Muslims are inferior to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not use that qualification myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to -- to now move to how you yourself describe Muslims in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But before I do, I'd like to tender that document, the "Informator."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 54 pages, Mr. Jeremy. Do we need them all?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we do need more than the sections that I've had the opportunity to read to the -- to the witness, but I agree that it is a long document and I would propose that it be MFI'd and I will take another look at the document and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- work to remove some sections before tendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you please do so because from my last question it appears that just reading it and associating this with the witness might not be fully fair to the witness. So therefore, if you limit yourself to put a few matters to say witness, then to say, well, the whole of it is in evidence may create a suggestion that, since he is on the cover page of this publication, that he would share all what's written in there and that would be perhaps not fully fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will wait for your further submissions as to what parts, and perhaps you also discuss the matter with Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would also note that the witness did say that he contributed to this publication. I accept he hasn't said he contributed to every page, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- that's how he's testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. That's exactly the reason why I'm cautious. We will hear from you but we already reserve a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 06616 receives P7015, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like now to take a look at your statement in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that's D861. And in particular I'd like to look at paragraph 7, please. It's page 3 in each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to focus your attention on -- I'd like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, the Chamber would like you to be aware that it found in paragraph 7 a lot of sweeping statements and not a lot of facts. That's how it was presented. And as you know, the Chamber is interested primarily in receiving evidence on facts and would certainly not encourage further detailed debates about sweeping statements, judgements, opinions, et cetera. Please keep that in the back of your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's understood, Your Honours, and my intention is simply to clarify some parts of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would like to focus on two aspects of this paragraph which I will read to you and then I will ask you some follow-up questions. Now, six or so lines down we read -- well, you refer to going to Muslim villages and speaking to the persons who were there. Now, I will read what you say in paragraph 7: "My main thesis was Muslims, such as Hudo Kurbegovic" -- excuse me. "My main thesis was that the Muslims, as Islamicized Serbs, this time as before, would heed the ill-intended West to inflict as much harm as possible on the Orthodox Serbs." And I'd also like to read you a part in the second half of the last sentence reading: "I also told them in advance that no matter how much they understood me at the time, the primal hatred that existed in them towards their kind from whom they broke away by changing religion would still heed the evil and cunning intentions of the West." Now, sir, when you -- when you refer in this paragraph to Muslim villages you're referring to Muslim villages in Sanski Most; yes?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you refer to primal hatreds, you're talking about primal hatreds in Muslims towards Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you were touring these Muslim villages in Sanski Most in April and May 1992; yes?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you were doing so in your capacity as assistant commander for morale and religious affairs in the 6th Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, I'd like to move on to a different topic. We can leave this paragraph. Now, sir, you are aware that in early November 1992, nine civilians from Skrljevita village were murdered in Sanski Most? Sir, should I repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should wait for the interpretation to be finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay, forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that in early November 1992, nine civilians from Skrljevita were murdered? They were shot. You're aware of that, yes?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that now. If there is a document or anything that would confirm that, perhaps I could. Is that the case where Danilusko committed these killings?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of them. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now having had your recollection refreshed, do you recall discussing this event at a meeting of the Sanski Most Executive Committee on the 10th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember. If there is a document that I could see, perhaps then I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at such a document. It's 65 ter 31785.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, while that's being brought up, I can tell you that they are the minutes of the extraordinary session of the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most, and they are dated the 10th of November, 1992. So, sir, on the screen before us we have those minutes. And we see that they are indeed dated the 10th of November, 1992, so nine days or so after the events in Skrljevita. And I will note that ten or so lines down we see -- we read that: "In addition to the members of the Executive Committee, the session was also attended by ..." And we have a list of attendees including Boro Tadic. That would have been you; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus your attention on some comments that we see from Mirko Vrucinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, Mirko Vrucinic was the chief of the Sanski Most Public Security Station; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in the third sentence below his name, we read that: "On the 1st of November, 1992, nine members of Skrljevita village were killed. They were ordinary people who were not extremists; the motive was retaliation for the fallen soldiers from Krihare." Now, sir, does that refresh your recollection of this meeting? I saw you -- you nodded, could you articulate an answer for the record?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm getting into this bit by bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 2 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you some comments from Vlado Vrkes. And these are near the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And five or six lines from below his name. We read --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, in the English it's two-thirds of the way down on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see there that he suggests that a visit should be paid to General Talic to inform him about all these acts, and we see that he says: "Proceedings have to be instituted against perpetrators of these unlawful acts." And I would like to look at the conclusions from this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could please go to page 4 in the English and 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And about halfway down the page we see a list of conclusions. I would like to focus on number 2, where we read: "Arrange a visit to the Command of the 1st Krajina Corps...," and "... inform the corps commander about the situation of the municipality ..." It goes on and lists the names of the delegation. And, Mr. Tadic, you're listed as one of those members of the delegation in your capacity as chief of the Sanski Most department of the Ministry of Defence. Can you confirm that you were in fact part of that delegation that went to see General Talic?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- yes, I heard the witness answer the question but there was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, that delegation discussed with General Talic these events in Skrljevita; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you recall General Talic's position in respect of these events?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, this Court has received evidence that of the four men accused of these events, two of them - Goran Vukojevic and Todo Vukic - were under 18 at the time of the events. So they were minors. Now, were you or are you aware that two of those men were under 18 at the time of these events in Skrljevita?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that I'm hearing of it. I mean, I didn't really follow that much. But any incident or any killing really caused me a lot of pain, not only because of the other peoples but also because of my own people, because of the fact that nothing would be left except evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to show you a document in connection with these two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we please see 65 ter 16467. And, Your Honours, I'd like to tender those minutes that we just saw, 65 ter 31785.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31785 receives Exhibit Number P7016, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7016 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, we see on our screens before us a document from the Banja Luka military court. It's dated the 9th of December, 1992. And we see in the top right corner of the original the stamp of the military prosecutor's office and the 1st Krajina Corps command. Now, in the first paragraph we -- we see that the investigating judge of the Banja Luka military court in the case of Kajtez et al. has decided to sever the case against Goran Vukojevic and Todo Vokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to page 2 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And next to Roman numeral II, halfway down the page in the B/C/S, towards the top of the page in the English, we read: "The severed case files relating to underage Goran Vukojevic and Todo Vokic are passed onto the authority of a judge for minors of the Sanski Most lower court for special proceedings pursuant to provisions in the 27th chapter of the Law on Criminal Procedure." Now, sir, seeing this document does that refresh your recollection about these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Actually, I only now understand it. I thought that we were talking about those who were killed but were under 18, but on the basis of this I understand that this is about those who actually committed the killing but were under 18. I don't know very much about it. I know very little about it. I was informed about it then at the Executive Board meeting, and I was in that delegation. And I'm sure I said the kind of things that I would say now, that this was a -- a major evil that we Serbs were committing against ourselves. I always said the same thing, and I can see that this was committed by two persons who were under 18. I'm only now getting that fact. But I really wasn't all that much involved in this because I was working in the Ministry of Defence section that was dealing with the mobilisation of people and assets, and I had so much work to do that I didn't have time to get involved in other things that were not part of my job description. But I welcomed every act that Republika Srpska carried out against the evil within ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned in your lengthy answer that you were, among other things, responsible for mobilisation. Now, you were aware or are you aware that despite the charges against Goran Vukojevic, he was the very next year mobilised into the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We did have records of young men who were 17 and recruited, and it's possible that he, like all the others, was entered into the records and recruited into the Army of Republika Srpska. This could easily be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to go to one such record, and before I do, Your Honours, could I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 16467 receives Exhibit Number P7017, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7017 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we please see 65 ter 06514.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, as this is being brought up I can tell you it's a stamped certificate issued by the RS Ministry of Defence, Sanski Most department certifying that Goran Vukojevic served in the forces in Banja Luka during a particular period. So we now have the certificate on the screen before us. And we see it is from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Defence, department of Sanski Most. We see the date is the 15th of December, 1994. And we see that it -- the document is issued at the request of Vukojevic, Goran, from Kruhari. And there is a certificate. It certified that Goran Vukojevic from Kruhari, born in 1975, served in the military service in the period from 18th of June, 1993, to the 21st of February, 1994. And his unit is listed. And we read that he is still engaged as a member of reserve formation. And we read that the certificate is issued and used for and then we read "justification of absence at the court procedure in Banja Luka," and it's signed by Chief Boro Tadic. So firstly, Mr. Tadic, do you recall signing this particular document?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I signed thousands of documents, but it's a sure thing that I did not sign anything that was inaccurate because I see on the basis of this that he served his regular term of duty and that he asked for leave and he was granted what he was requesting. And it's true that according to this document he did serve his regular military term of duty in that time-period, and perhaps he was getting summonses, but it seems that he needed that in order for him to justify his absence from the trial. But I see that this certificate was issued with that intention. But it does confirm the fact that during that time-period he was a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
