utterances.text: So, sir, on the basis of your answer do I understand it correctly that it was the case that even if criminal proceedings had been initiated against you for an event as serious as the events in Skrljevita, military service could excuse you from those proceedings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: A witness is not somebody -- oh, a person is not guilty unless it's proven or unless they've been sentenced. So they are expected to carry out their regular duties, the things they need to do in life. And probably because he was not in detention, he was free, and so he could not have been considered guilty, regardless of the indictment, until the trial had been finished. So if he had responded to the summons, he did what he needed to do. Had he been in detention, had he been in investigative prison, then this kind of thing could not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But, sir, this document, as I read it, is justifying the absence of Goran Vukojevic from the court procedure in Banja Luka. So at least on face value it suggests to me that there were proceedings that were going on but Mr. Vukojevic wasn't present at those proceedings because instead he was serving in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Probably he was summoned during the time that he was serving his military term of duty. I cannot remember the details right now. But by that logic, while he was serving in the military he received a summons. That is what would be logical. But I cannot recall any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But, sir, my question very simply is: The fact is -- if he did receive a summons, was the fact that he was serving in the military a sufficient reason for him not to respond to that summons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking for judgement, Mr. Jeremy. So please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm actually prepared to rely on the answers that I've already got from the witness on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then put your next question to the witness. Perhaps after the break because we're at the time for a break. Are you on schedule as far as time is concerned, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I estimated two and a half hours and I hope I will come in somewhere under that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You indicated two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's at least what was our information, that you asked for two hours, but please verify that. And I do understand that you would certainly not need two and a half hours, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you tender this document which is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06514 receives Exhibit P7018, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7018 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Tadic, we would like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to respond to the question that you asked of me a moment ago. We revised the time for this witness up to two and a half hours via e-mail on the 10th of December at 1528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we may have missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- an informal communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We may have missed that. And we'll now take a break and the time estimate is that we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I mistakenly understood or assumed that you had been advised that there were two preliminary matters and I'm very sorry about that. One of those should be raised in private session. If it's too late now, we can do it at the next session. But in any event, there will be two matters to raise in response -- both of which are in response to earlier Court inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it's not the best moment to -- when the witness will enter the courtroom, but perhaps we could take the next break a bit earlier and then do it at the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just to make you aware, during this session it may be that I ask you to draw the witness's attention to his rights under Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just indicate the moment. As you know that we usually leave it to the parties who know what questions will be put to the witness, whether it's appropriate or not to give him a 90(E) warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, for planning purposes I anticipate finishing within under 45 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we would still have time for the other matters. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, the civilian protection staff in Sanski Most formed part of the national defence and were therefore part of your responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And among other things, the civilian protection staff were responsible for burials of human remains found in Sanski Most during the war period; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: We have to differentiate here. I was responsible for mobilisation of personnel and material assets for the civilian protection, but I was not authorised to decide on the use of civilian protection units or those of the army or those for the obligatory work duty. So my job was to provide the personnel or assets to the civilian protection army and the work-duty units, but those who were carrying out their orders received from higher levels would carry out the assignments. This applied to the army, which had its command, to the enterprises, which had their directors and management system, and the same applied to the civilian protection, which had its own commander who carried out these duties pursuant to the law and the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But, sir, generally speaking, you were aware of the activities that were carried out by the civilian protection force in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Sometimes I would be there at a briefing when civilian protection tasks were discussed at the Executive Board. Since I attended the Executive Board sessions only when it pertained to things that had to do with the Ministry of Defence, it's possible that I was sometimes present when issues regarding the use of civilian protection were discussed. I'm not quite sure about it right now. I don't recall the details, but perhaps if there are any documents you can show me, then perhaps we could discuss those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a look at some documents, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the first one, please, is 65 ter 06444.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And while this is being brought up, Mr. Tadic, I can tell you that it's a report about activities of civilian protection headquarters Sanski Most municipality during the period from 15th of July, 1992, to the 15th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, could we please go to page 3 in each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tadic, as you'll see, the B/C/S document is not as legible as one would hope, so I'd ask you for your patience. Now, sir, I'd like to direct your attention to the paragraph numbered number 1 towards the top of the page: "Demolition and sanitation of residential buildings." Now, we see a reference to a joint action of the civilian protection staff and the municipal Ministry for National Defence connecting to a list being made of able-bodied men between 17 to 60. That reference to the municipal Ministry for National Defence, that was part of your responsibility; correct? That's a reference to your department. I see you're nodding. Could you verbalize --

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: This is a confirmation of what I have just said. It was my duty to note down the population that could become part or used in the work of the civilian protection. The mobilising of them and passing them on to the units of civilian protection or the civilian protection commander so that they could be used, that was my part. And this is confirmed by this paragraph here, that we did this in co-operation. We worked together on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we please zoom in on paragraph -- this paragraph 1, please; particularly, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to look at the last sentence of that. If you can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we perhaps widen the page a little bit, if possible, for the B/C/S. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, it reads as follows: "The brigades worked on the demolition and sanitation of residential and religious buildings in the following inhabited areas." Now, the religious buildings being referred to here are mosques; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I cannot see it here. Is that paragraph 1, item 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It's the last sentence of paragraph 1 towards the top of the page. Sir, if you can't read that sentence, then I won't ask you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: The only thing that I can say, judging by what I understand here, even though you can't even read it, is that those units were engaged on clearing up the consequences of something that was done. For example, something that was beyond repair. It was demolished, needed to be cleared up so that it would not pose a danger to the people. And the things that could be repaired would be repaired. This is how I understood it. The demolition and sanitation of -- so something that had already been demolished in an action by whoever did that. So that there would be no safety problems, it had to be completely demolished if it couldn't be used anymore or it could not be rebuilt; whereas things that were just slightly damaged could be repaired and used again. This is how I understood what is written -- how I understand what is written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, actually you're not being asked to tell us what you understand but tell us what you read there if you are able to read it. We can always give the interpretations that we want to give, but the question really is, and the answer should be very short: Can you read it, and read it if you can. Because now you are putting words into this statement which are not there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The demolition and sanitation of housing and religious buildings ..." And now there is a part that's difficult. It says "brigades" but this other word is difficult. "Construction." I think that's what it says. "Construction Brigade" or "Brigades," something like that. "Housing Units, Construction Brigades." Something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, this Trial Chamber has received evidence that at least 18 mosques were destroyed in Sanski Most during the period of 1992 to 1995. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I was. And I passed by and I could see demolished mosques. I did witness that mosques were demolished. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you see who it was who demolished those mosques?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to look at another part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that's in the paragraph below the one that we've just been looking at. And unfortunately, it's also not the clearest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- just before B on the screen, there is a sentence that I would like to -- to read -- or I'll read a few sentences up from there, and the subheading of this paragraph is: "In the Town." So we read: "Simultaneously with these activities a considerable amount of time was spent removing debris from the town mosque. These activities are still underway and the exhumation and dislocation of the cemetery next to the town mosque will begin after the adoption of appropriate decisions in the municipal assembly. The machinery that exists in the 6th Brigade was also used in these activities." So, sir, we see here that the civil protection headquarters of Sanski Most is anticipating a decision in the municipal assembly to exhume and dislocate the cemetery next to the town mosque. Now, my first question: That cemetery was a Muslim cemetery; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably, next to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the decision to exhume that cemetery was, in fact, subsequently taken in February 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It's possible. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But before I do, Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document but I -- because the B/C/S is illegible, then I would propose that we MFI the document and we'll -- I will go into the evidence unit and try and find a more legible document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be appreciated. Apparently someone was able to read it, otherwise you couldn't translate it. And -- but, as you are suggesting, we'll MFI it. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06444 receives P7019, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is marked for identification. Witness, the last question was about a decision taken in February 1993 to exhume and relocate. You said you don't remember. Don't you remember the date or don't you remember that such a decision was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not a member of the assembly. I wasn't a member of the party, of any other party, neither the Serbian Democratic Party or any other political party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I was not asking whether you were a member of a party. I was asking you whether you were uncertain about that such a decision was taken, sometimes you can know that even if you are not a member of the organ that takes a decision, or that you are uncertain about the date. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about how I didn't attend sessions very often. I could have been invited only when questions were discussed from my remit. So I cannot remember this, unless there is a document that would help me to remember what that was about. I was not a member of the assembly. I only attended when I was summoned, when issues were discussed that I was responsible for. I mean, it's possible that I did attend. But if there is a document, then I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it is about whether you knew, not about were you responsible, whether or not you attended. Do you know that a decision was taken or do you not know? Your memory --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, I will see if I can refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31788.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, coming on to our screens are the minutes of the 7th Session of the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most. And they are dated the 25th of February, 1993. We see those minutes on the screen before us. And I note in the fourth paragraph that: "In addition to the members of the Executive Committee, the following invitees were present ..." And the penultimate name is Boro Tadic. Now, sir, that would have been you; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 3 of these minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, my first question. Just above item 3, we see the final bullet point is that the work of commission be updated regarding the changing of the street names, squares, and public institutions. Sir, this is a reference to changing the street names, squares, and public institutions that contained Muslim names to Serb names; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. Everybody did that in the same way. Muslims would delete Serb names and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you about what you did in Sanski Most and what this executive body did. So is that what they are indeed doing, they are changing names from Muslim origin to Serb names?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: That was updating the work of the -- of the commission for renaming of the streets. I don't know whether it was ever done. I suppose there is a report to that effect, to show whether the update was implemented or not. This is just about the updating of the work of that commission. Effectively, it was operational, it existed, and its work was being updated with this. This is how I understand things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I understand it's a reference to an update. But just very simply, when you read this reference to the changing of street names, squares, and public institutions, do you understand this to be the changing of those names from Muslim names to Serb names?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I suppose that there were such cases as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 7 in the English and 6 in the B/C/S. And I would like to focus on item 9 when we get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, under item 9, sir, we read: "The Chairman opened the discussion topic - endorsing draft decision on exhumation of mortal remains from the cemetery in the Centre (next to the mosque) and the cemetery in Zdena (in the vicinity of Sip). "Since there were no participants in the discussion, pursuant to the proposal of the Chairman, the Executive Committee made the following conclusion: "1. The draft decision on exhumation of mortal remains from the cemetery in the centre (next to the mosque) and the cemetery in Zdena (in the vicinity of Sip) is endorsed." Mr. Tadic, the locations referred to here are Muslim cemeteries; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the goal of this decision was to remove traces of Muslims in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I don't know the details. For some reason that was done. But about destroying any traces, you can't destroy traces, can you? I really don't see it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you have any doubts, what, in your view, was the reason to do this? What was discussed or not discussed? What was the underlying reason to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really was not that much involved in all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no idea, although it was scheduled that meeting, it apparently was an issue that was decided there, but you say: I've got no idea what it was for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no discussion at all. There was never a discussion on that issue. And why things were done, if they were, I don't know any details. It was not within my remit and I didn't get involved in all that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about details. I'm asking about what the purpose of exhumation of mortal remains was, from these cemeteries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you were taken by surprise. You have no idea why -- well, quite an operational thing would have happened at that point in time with that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we look at the list of attendees of this meeting, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. Could we go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you say you were not involved in this. You were not part of it. But were you not a member of this meeting, were you not a part of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was invited to the meeting of the Executive Board because of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you how -- just hold it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- item 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just hold it. I'm not asking you how you came there, whether by invitation or what. You were part of the meeting, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And you -- and part of the meeting endorsed the decision, whether it was discussed or not discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not vote. I was a guest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether you voted. I'm saying the meeting endorsed that decision, although it was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, you can see that from the record of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to tender those minutes as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31788 receives Exhibit P7020, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tadic, given your responsibilities, were you aware that in 1994 the Banja Luka State Security Department also suggested that efforts were made to excavate Muslim mass graves?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I'm puzzled by the use of the word "also." We saw a decision on exhumation of mortal remains from a cemetery, not from any mass graves. So the "also" in the mass grave puzzles me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I'd just rephrase the question and I remove the "also" reference which I concede was misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, given your responsibilities, were you aware that in 1994, the Banja Luka State Security Department suggested that efforts were made to excavate Muslim mass graves?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not abreast of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we see 65 ter 31795.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, on our screens is a document from the state security department of Banja Luka, Prijedor detachment, and we see that it's dated 28th of March, 1994. And it's an Official Note. Now, in the first paragraph we read that: "During 1992 there were several armed clashes with Muslim paramilitary formations in the Sanski Most area, concentrated mainly in the villages of Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, Trnovo, Lukavica, and Modra." Now, sir, you were aware of those locations in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I know. I know these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I understand from your Karadzic testimony that you were not present during the operations by the 6th Brigade at the end of May and at the start of June in, for example, Vrhpolje and Hrustovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now in the next paragraph we see the following. We see a reference to Muslim extremists who have moved members of their family to other areas before the outbreak of those clashes, and we read that they were killed in this fighting. We read: "Because of this, they were buried in common graves by members of their own people, neighbours, and other people employed by the competent organs." Now, those "other persons employed by the competent organs" would have included the civil defence, civil protection unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I can't say anything. I guess that organisation was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we read: "Following the cessation of fighting in these areas, some people took part in burying those killed left our area in convoys, on release from the Manjaca camp and in other ways." And it goes on to say that their information has been used as Muslim propaganda, Muslim media propaganda to increase pressure against Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the final sentence we read that the -- the state security department measures, as a suggestion we read: To counter such occurrences and to prevent in good time the use of such events for propaganda purposes and pressure on the Serbian people, we believe that it is necessary to suggest that the relevant institutions activate the competent organs in Sanski Most to sanitize the locations in question. Now, sir, this last paragraph is about hiding Muslim mass graves; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: That's one way of interpreting it. However, I was not at all the involved in all that. Therefore, I have nothing to say about it. There was a lot of propaganda, that is true. And every shortcoming on our side - and there was some, of course - was used in propaganda and to increase pressure on the Serbian people instead of those who created the evil and caused the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was about what was envisaged to be done. Your answer is not about that apart from the beginning where you said: "That's one way of interpreting it." However, you were not at all involved in that. May I take it then also that you mean to say by that that you have no knowledge about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. Because this word, "sanitization" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you don't remember, you don't remember. You don't have to explain why you don't remember. You don't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31795 receives Exhibit Number P7021, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tadic, in your capacity as the head of the Ministry of Defence in -- of Republika Srpska in Sanski Most, you were responsible for work obligation in the municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And those non-Serbs that remained in Sanski Most during the war period were subject to the work obligation; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: For a while they were not. Security conditions would not allow for that. When it was decided that things could be arranged and that people could be engaged safely, the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska issued an order to that effect. There were priorly set up obligation units and Serbs were mobilised into companies and institutions and so on and so forth. However, when it was assessed that Muslims and Croats could be engaged and that security issues could easily be avoided, that no major incidents could be expected, we wanted to include them and incorporate them to everyday life.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at a document in connection with those duties that you performed and in relation to these work obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31792.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a report which I think you'll recognise. It's dated the 5th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2, please, in each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, we see your name at the bottom of the page and your signature. Do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, we see that this is a letter from the RS Ministry of Defence, Banja Luka district, department of Sanski Most. Dated the 5th of October, 1994. It's addressed to the Executive Board of Sanski Most municipality -- sorry, Municipal Assembly, and to the command of the Sana 6th Infantry Brigade. Now, the subject is: "Deployment of Work Obligation Units." I would like to look at one or two paragraphs of this document. In the first paragraph we read that: "Over the past 16 months, the Ministry of Defence Department of Sanski Most has deployed work obligation units consisting of non-Serbs, as requested by the VRS and various enterprises, institutions, and individuals." In the next paragraph, in the second sentence, we read that: "... units comprising non-Serbs began to be utilised," and in the sentence before we see from May 1993, "while the other units made up of Serbs never were." And now, sir, you were responsible for this -- these mobilisations of these non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: This is about me being tasked with mobilising people with -- talking to them about their future work. And in the second text, it says that the utilisation of those units should be handed over to the Executive Board because, pursuant to that order, they were supposed to implement that work. We were in charge of mobilising and sending people to various places on requests by the military, by the civilian protection, by various institutions and so on and so forth. And here, I really don't understand this sentence. I know that Serbs were utilised. I don't see why it says "while the other units made up of Serbs never were." I really can't make a logical link because I know that there were, i.e. the Serbs were, in work obligation units and they were deployed wherever needed in all the institutions that requested them; whereas Muslims were not before the conditions were put in place for them to participate without expecting any major issues. That is why the units that had been set up were dispatched on the requests of the military, companies, and other institutions. And here the point of all this, of this report, is that the Executive Board should be more involved in the utilisation of those units. I can see that there were not enough people employed for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any reason to doubt the authenticity of the original document that you see on the screen before you, the copy of the original document?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't have a reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, could we please go to page 3 in each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a table and it is headed: "Overview of Deployment of the Work Obligation Units Composed of Non-Serbs in the Municipality of Sanski Most." And down the left side we see the various locations from which non-Serbs originated and the right side we see the total of those persons from those locations and that total runs into the hundreds. Now, sir, it was your task to select from the available population of non-Serbs in Sanski Most those persons who you considered fit for various jobs and to send them along to perform those jobs; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, before I ask the witness the next question, I wonder if it's -- I'd ask that you inform the witness of his rights --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- under Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, in view of the next questions that will be put to you, Mr. Jeremy asked me to inform you about the following. Rule 90(E) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence reads as follows: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." In short, if a truthful answer to any of the questions that will follow would possibly be incriminating for yourself, you may address me and ask to be relieved from answering that question. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tadic, of the jobs that you sent non-Serbs to complete, you sent a number of those non-Serbs to the front line to, for example, dig trenches, and in doing so you sent many non-Serbs to their deaths; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It is just like using a Serb to send him to the army. It was wartime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and there was a need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, simple question: Did you send a number of those non-Serbs to the front line? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, sending somebody to the regular military. Now, where that person is going to be utilised, it's up to the military. It was at the request of the military, a certain number of people were engaged and sent to various commands. For example, companies, both socially owned and private companies, relied on the same system. Just like Serbs were mobilised into the military, Muslims, Croats, or whoever were mobilised at the request of the army, and they were handed over to the organisation that requested them, either the military or a private company or a socially owned company. From that moment on it is those companies that requested them that decided how to use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would they -- a number of them be sent to the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite possible. It is possible that they were used by the military for certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Either the delivery of food and water or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, that's not what you were asked. So you say it's possible that they were sent to the front. Do you have any knowledge whether they were sent there and had to dig trenches? If you have knowledge, please tell us. If you don't have any knowledge, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that they were deployed in that way, but I don't know anything specific. I know that I handed them over to the military, to be used by the military. And it says in this table here. It says in the table the military, the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "I know they were deployed in that way ..." My question was about digging trenches. Do I understand you to say that they were deployed in, perhaps among other things, also in digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no knowledge, no details. I can't confirm any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the last part of the question was whether you know whether some persons sent to the military under this work obligation, whether they did not return because they died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Many returned -- actually, many dead Serbian soldiers returned. There were many things going on on a daily basis. People being killed left and right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, why not answer my question. My question was whether some of those who were sent there under the work obligation to the army, whether some of them did not return because they died. I am not asking who returned, but I'm asking whether some did not return because they had died when fulfilling that obligation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've no specific knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you earlier confirmed today that you testified in the Karadzic case and that the answers you gave in that case were truthful. I'd like to show you a portion of your testimony in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31781 on our screens. And I'd like to tender the document we were just looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31792 receives Exhibit Number P7022, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we go to page 48, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm afraid we don't have a B/C/S translation of this transcript, so you'll need to listen to the translation. I'll read out the portion I want you to pay attention to and it will be translated to you. And, sir, I'm going to focus on questions that were put to you in relation to the same document that we have just looked at, just one question and your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So if we could focus on -- into line 7 and below, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see that the Prosecutor asked you the following question: "Q. Sending them wherever they were needed included sending them to the front line and sending them to clear minefields and sending them to their deaths; isn't that correct?" Your answer: "I sent many more Serbs to their deaths. This is all about 113 people being sent to the front line. We, however, sent thousands upon thousands to the front lines. If I sent thousands of Serbs to the front line, why wouldn't I send a hundred Muslims to carry water, to dig trenches, and so on and so forth?" And I'll end it there. So do you stand by the answer that you provided in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: The use of those units was defined by order --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I mobilised --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- I'm very sorry to interrupt you. But just very simply: Was the answer that you gave during your testimony in the Karadzic case truthful and do you stand by that answer today?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: My answer was truthful. When discussing the topic where I was more tense than I am now, I said that the use of such units for work obligation was logical in my view so that Muslims and Croats, too, would be included in the events, given the fact that there was war, and they were simply made part of the defence system. They were not given weapons so as not to be forced to shoot at their compatriots but to assist the army in the performance of its tasks. As per order which I received, that's how things were implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So your answer was truthful and you stand by that in this courtroom; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, my final question: In your statement in paragraph 9, you refer to respect for humanitarian law and the laws of war, and in particular the Geneva Conventions. Now, do you consider sending non-Serbs to the front lines to be consistent and compatible with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It depends on the manner of use.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: If they were indeed used as a human shield, that would be against the conventions. But if they were used to bring water and food and to assist with noncombat tasks, that would not fall under that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: So it's important that they are not used as a human shield, as someone who would be directly exposed to enemy attack. I certainly hope that there were no such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, sending Serbs [sic] to the front lines to dig trenches, as you said in the Karadzic case and you've repeated here, do you consider that to be consistent with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: The sending of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The sending of non-Serbs was my question, or it should have been.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It was interpreted to me as "the Serbs." In my view, any inhumane treatment, including exposing someone to enemy fire, would be in contravention of God's law and human law, thus being against the Geneva Convention. I condemn any exposure of such people to a danger of being killed by the enemy side. In my view, it would cause great damage to the Serb people and the Army of Republika Srpska. I therefore engaged those people as per army request under the understanding that they would be used in a way that would not threaten their life and security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I will stop you again. After ten lines you've still not answered the question. Do you consider digging trenches to be among -- digging trenches by non-Serbs, do you consider that to be in violation of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does if they are exposed to direct gun-fire and in a position to be killed. So the difference is in how they're used and what the assessment of the officer concerned was at that moment, whether they were wilfully putting those people in danger to be killed. If that was the intent of the officer concerned, then that would be against the conventions. But if their security was borne in mind and if they were used only for tasks that would not endanger their lives, in my view that would not be against the rules as envisaged. The intention was not to use those people so as to protect Serbian lives. That would not have been a good situation. I would never have participated in any such thing had I had any knowledge of any such use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you draw a very fine line, digging trenches with danger and digging trenches without danger of being fired at. Could you tell us where in the Geneva Conventions you find the basis for this distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I make that distinction in my heart of hearts. If Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. So it means that you make that distinction --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The intent is key.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, I was asking you where in the Geneva Conventions you find the basis for making that distinction and your answer tells me that it was not actually on the basis of the Geneva Conventions that you made that distinction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, that was your last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It was, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, could you tell us, we'll take a break, but how much time you would need after the break? And meanwhile, the witness can be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to count my questions. Probably I should finish in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it makes sense to keep the next witness to remain standby. No. Perhaps you need to make some submissions. I have to read two decisions. Perhaps we do that to start with after the break. Then we would conclude the evidence of this witness today. And then tomorrow the time schedule was, I think, half an hour for the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- two hours for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which makes two and a half hours. I would expect the parties to do their utmost best to conclude the evidence of the next witness by tomorrow as well so that he doesn't have to return after many, many weeks. Yes. Then the witness who is at this moment on standby for tomorrow can be -- doesn't need to remain standby and is expected to be here tomorrow at 9.30. We take a break and will resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Lukic. May I again remind you that you are expected to answer the question, first of all. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon yet again, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Godspeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not have much time and yet we have to conclude, so I would kindly ask for brief answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have P7016, please, on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic, you were shown these minutes from the extraordinary meeting of the Executive Committee, and we saw already that you were in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the next page -- in the B/C/S it is actually the next page and in English it is the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were told that on the 1st of November, 1992, which is at the top of the page, nine members from Skrljevita were killed. A conclusion was reached --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, page 4; in B/C/S, 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- to the effect that General Talic should be informed accordingly. You were a member of the commission. Do you remember what you were told? Were you told to cover anything up or to go public with it or to speak to Talic or to demand action? What was the task you received?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I do not recall the details, but as far as I can remember there was nothing to hide and that's what I firmly believe in. God sees everything and people can only try hiding things but to no avail. That is why it was useful to discuss any evil that we may have perpetrated upon another. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at P7017, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is a decision to separate or split up proceedings. It is not on the screen yet. It concerns minors Goran Vukojevic and Todo Vokic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Goran Vukojevic and Todo Vokic."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was established that on that given date they were minors. As such, could they have been mobilised in the JNA or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Later, yes, once they reached their 18th birthday, but not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at P7020.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is the minutes of the 7th Session of the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most. We see your name appearing on the first page; thus, you were in attendance with the members of the Executive Committee. In item 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S it is page 6, in the English version, page 7. Just to remind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Item 9, point 1, it reads: "A draft decision on the exhumation of mortal remains from the cemetery in the town centre ... and the cemetery in Zdena" is thus endorsed. Is Zdena a village?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It is in the outskirts of the town. It is a settlement, part of the town in the outskirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the municipality of Sanski Most, were these the only two Muslim cemeteries?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: No, there were many, many more. I don't know how many exactly but around 50 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see in item 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the previous question was about the municipality of Sanski Most. How many Muslim cemeteries were there in the town of Sanski Most, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hail from Palanka, 25 kilometres to the west, so I don't know Sanski Most in detail. Around a dozen in all likelihood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's a calculated guess I then take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have no other means of calculating it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, would you say that even if these two cemeteries were completely destroyed and eradicated, would that have done away with all traces of Muslim cemeteries in the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Definitely not, and that was certainly not the intention. I can't remember what the reason was, though. There must be one but I don't remember it. In any case, this was not the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under 4 in the same document - we have it on our screens - we can see that the chairman called the meeting to order and spoke about the record of military conscripts. It says here that Boro Tadic spoke about the record that had been established by way of introduction. Was that your main role at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And there was always a struggle as to how many people should be kept in companies and how many should be sent to the theatre of war, and we can see that people in the companies wanted to keep as many people as possible in order to maintain production, and the military wanted their share. So there was always a struggle between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know whether you remember whether you stayed at the very end of the session. Would you usually stay until the end or would you leave after submitting your report?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I probably left because I attended only as a guest only because of the item that I reported on. I was not a member of the Executive Board, and if I'd stayed, I would have had to get involved and discuss issues under other items of the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at P7022 for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It will be the last document that I intend to show you. My learned friend Mr. Jeremy showed you this document about the deployment of work obligation units. We saw your signature at the end of page 2. But before that, we have a list of those who were deployed; i.e., those who had been mobilised. At that time under the law, were Muslims and Croats exempt from mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: No, they were citizens of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were a battalion commander in Croatia. In Croatia did Serbian soldiers dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Serbian soldiers were digging trenches in the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I was not a commander there, but I suppose that they did dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we continue in this line, is the underlying thought that soldiers would not dig trenches for their own army?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, it's absolutely not. No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's normal that somebody who is mobilised should dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I said to the first line, so it's normal for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Then I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you were in the process of creating those work obligation units, were there any interventions by Serbs to be transferred from war units to work obligation units? We have not discussed that ever before. I'm asking you now.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of pressure put on me to bear. Many wanted not to be in the army for various reasons. And then when they had spoken with their company directors and agreed on certain things, they would put pressure on me to include them in a work obligation unit in that company. You can see, for example, Srecko Bulj [phoen], who spoke at that session, insisted to have as many people in the company who would work for him. There was a constant pressure put on me to bear to move people from war units to work obligation units to the companies that wanted to maintain their production. It was a constant tug-of-war, a constant pressure put on me to bear to strike a certain balance. On the one hand, there was the military who wanted to have as many military conscripts for war operations, the brigades were deployed all over the place; and on the other hand, there were the needs of the companies and municipalities to maintain production and to have as many assets as possible in operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can tell us or whether -- if you can tell us -- if you can assess what was safer: To be a member of a war unit or a work obligation unit?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: It was much safer to be in a work obligation unit than in a war unit. And one of the reasons for all that pressure is not just the need of the companies but also fear from the whirlwind of war and possible death on the first line. Many wanted to be exempted from that rather than to resort to desertion from a military unit. There was a lot of pressure put on me to bear by people who wanted to save themselves from the first line and to be safer in a work obligation unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, thank you. That was all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Jeremy:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Actually, could we have on our screens P7020, please. Those are the minutes of the 7th Session of the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, Mr. Tadic, as those minutes are coming up, Mr. Lukic a moment ago asked you whether you remember whether you stayed at the very end of this session and whether you'd usually stay until the end or whether you would leave after you submitting your report, and you said that actually -- you said that: "I probably left because I attended only as a guest ..." Now, sir, I just want to draw your attention to the agenda, point 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we see there the agenda, point 9, endorsing draft decision on exhumation of mortal remains. And it goes on to refer to the cemeteries we've been discussing. So you would have been there at that point when you -- at least during that point when that agenda item was raised; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I can see that my item is under 4, so I really can't remember whether I stayed until the very end. There were cases when I did stay, but there were also other cases when I left sessions after having intervened under my item of the agenda for previous commitments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that. But these are minutes of the session that you attended, and what I'm saying to you is at the very start of those minutes, an agenda item, point 9, was read out relating to this exhumation of these graves, and I'm asking you if it's likely that you would have been present when these agenda items were read out before you spoke at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Quite possible but I can't remember. There were many of those. I can't remember. But it was also common for me to leave earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: BORO TADIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. No further questions by the Bench. Mr. Tadic, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I wish all of you all the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a few minutes left. We first move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No other issues. Then I would like to read, and that might go a couple of minutes beyond the time, but I nevertheless hope that, with the assistance of the interpreters and all others who are assisting us, will not -- we'll not stop halfway. First is the decision on the admission of P6682, which is a collection of Council of Europe reports which were marked for identification pending a possible agreement by the parties. This can be found at transcript pages 24243 to 24252, and page 24270. An agreement between the parties was not reached. The Defence filed its written submissions on the 23rd of September, 2014. The Defence requests the Chamber -- request that the Chamber deny the report's admission into evidence. It argues, inter alia, that it is improper for the Prosecution to present positive evidence subsequent to the close of its case. The document does not meet the criteria for admission via cross-examination, and the document contains over 400 pages with no witness to authenticate or explain the content. The Defence submits that the subject matter of the document goes beyond the witness's knowledge and testimony and contains information related to geographical areas also outside the scope of the indictment. Further, the Defence submits that certain parts of the document rely on hearsay and rumours, and that no information is provided on the sources or methodology to ensure the document's reliability. The Prosecution responded on the 3rd of October, 2014, submitting that the pages of the report which it tenders are relevant and probative; thus, meeting the requirements of Rule 89(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecution submits that the tendered pages of the report are relevant to the destruction of mosques in Foca municipality, which forms part of the indictment against the accused. According to the Prosecution, the report has probative value and contains information regarding its provenance and reliability. The Prosecution submits, inter alia, that the Defence's arguments should be rejected because no legal authority has been cited, and the arguments go to weight as opposed to admissibility. Further, the Prosecution submits that the Defence's arguments regarding its tendering of evidence during cross-examination have previously been rejected by this Chamber. At the outset, the Chamber notes that the Defence's submissions lack any reference to or discussion of the applicable law concerning the admission of evidence and are therefore completely unsupported. Moreover, with regard to the Defence's submission that it is improper for the Prosecution to present positive evidence after the close of its case, the Chamber recalls that in this regard on the 16th of September, 2014, it referred the parties to a decision in the Stanisic and Simatovic case dated the 26th of August, 2011. The Chamber thus dismisses the Defence's submission that the Prosecution should not be allowed to tender Exhibit P6682 subsequent to the close of its case. The Chamber recalls that the applicable law for the admission of evidence is Rule 89(C) of the Rules which allows a Chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. The Chamber does not consider the criteria submitted by the Defence for admission via cross-examination to be relevant in this context and thus dismisses the Defence's argument regarding the same. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution has only requested the admission of 13 pages in total. Therefore, the Chamber considers that the Defence's argument relating to the length of the document and that it also relates to areas outside the scope of the indictment is moot. The Chamber notes that Witness Vujicic provided some information regarding the destruction of mosques in Foca. The Prosecution discussed with the witness a list in the report of mosques purportedly destroyed in Foca. The Chamber considers this evidence to be relevant to scheduled incident D5. With regard to the relevant pages of the report tendered by the Prosecution, the Chamber is of the opinion that the sources of the list are not entirely clear and that some of the language used therein is ambiguous. The Chamber will, also in light of other evidence before it, take such factors into consideration when deciding the weight to be given to the document, but considers that there is sufficient information regarding the authors, sources of information, and the methodology used for the purposes of admission. The Chamber therefore finds that the tendered pages of the report are relevant and of probative value. With regard to the other arguments raised by the Defence, the Chamber considers that these go to the weight of the document rather than its admissibility. The Chamber therefore admits into evidence pages 1, 6 through 9, 12 through 14, and 32 through 36 of P6682. The Prosecution is instructed to upload a new version of P6682 reflecting the Chamber's decision, and the Registry is instructed to make the necessary replacement thereafter. The Prosecution is invited to upload a B/C/S version of the same, and the Registry is instructed to attach the translation to P6682 when it becomes available. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission of P6682. I'll not bother you with the other decision at this moment. We'll hopefully find time for that one tomorrow. We adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 18th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
